text.p: The unexpected departure of W.H.Smith Group Plc chief executive Bill Cockburn, announced on Monday, had nothing to do with problems at the retailing group, chairman Jeremy Hardie told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Hardie said Cockburn, who will leave Smith's in October after only 18 months as chief executive to join British Telecommunications Plc, had received an "irresistible" offer from BT and his decision to leave did not reflect any difficutlies at W.H.Smith.
"It's not to do with any problems, it's to do with an irresistible offer," Hardie said.
Cockburn also told Reuters the decision to leave was "all to do with this glittering opportunity at BT and mustn't be interpreted that there are problems here."
Cockburn said BT had approached him and offered the job of managing director of BT in the UK, which was to good an offer to turn down.
Cockburn said he would be running BT in the UK after the company completes its merger with U.S. telecoms group MCI Communications Corp.
He said W.H. Smith's new management team, including Beverley Hodson, the newly appointed managing director of the core retail chain, were well positioned to drive the business forward.
Cockburn, who joined W.H. Smith in November 1995, was brought in to overhaul the group which last summer reported its first loss in more than 200 years of retailing.

Under his management, Smith sold off non-core businesses including Do It All, the home improvement chain, and Business Supplies. The company made a profit in the first half, but retail analysts have remained concerned about the long term future of the core W.H. Smith chain.

These stores have faced increasingly cut-throat competition from food superstores as well as other "high street" retailers selling broadly the same range of goods - books, newspapers, magazines, videos, recorded music and greeting cards.

Cockburn acknowledged there was more to do in terms of the high street chain, but insisted it had tremendous strengths. "It's a very strong brand, it's going to be around for a very long time," he said.
Hardie said the group was already looking for a replacement for Cockburn, but declined to speculate on how long it might take.
There had been speculation about management discontent in the British press after the departure of Smith's commercial director Brent Wilkinson earlier this month.
Cockburn dismissed the speculation saying the senior management team running W.H.Smith retail were "absolutely united in implementing the strategy for success."
He said Hodson had decided to focus more closely on the commercial side of the business and she had a very clear programme of action.
W.H.Smith also said its results for the year to March 31, 1997 would be within the range of market expectations, which are for pre-tax profits of around 125 million stg.
In the first half Smith's pre-tax profits more than doubled to 38.6 million stg, but sales at the core chain were up just 1.5 percent.

Hardie said finance director Keith Hamill would brief analysts at 0900 GMT in more detail on the group's performance before it goes into "closed season" ahead of results, due to be published on August 27.
